vulnerabilities.details: Antiword through 0.37 contains a heap out-of-bounds read vulnerability in vGet8LstInfo in prop8.c caused by an inverted bounds check on the PlcfLst record count. Attackers can supply a crafted Word 8 .doc file claiming up to 0xffff LSTF records in a tiny buffer, causing reads past the heap allocation that crash the process.

Antiword through 0.37 contains a stack out-of-bounds read vulnerability in vGet8PapInfo and vGet8ChrInfo in prop8.c because FKP run counts and grpprl offsets are not bounded. Attackers can supply a crafted .doc file with malicious FKP pages to read past the 512-byte stack buffer, crashing antiword or corrupting style parsing.

vulnerabilities.details: On Debian, Ubuntu, and derivative Linux distributions, an on-path attacker who can manipulate the HTTP traffic (including a malicious mirror or proxy) between an APT client and an archive server triggered by a package install can trick the client into installing an attacker-controlled unverified package and achieve remote code execution with root privileges. The vulnerability is caused by the reuse of hard links and requires the client to follow redirects and retry the download of package files. It requires the client to have a non-zero Acquire::Retries configuration setting; the value 3 is the default starting with Debian 12 (bookworm) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish), so older releases are unaffected in a default configuration.

The C++ symbol demangler routine in cplus-dem.c in libiberty, as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive memory allocation and application crash) via a crafted file, as demonstrated by a call from the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd).

A vulnerability was found in GNU Binutils 2.43. It has been classified as problematic. This affects the function xstrdup of the file libiberty/xmalloc.c of the component ld. The manipulation leads to memory leak. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The complexity of an attack is rather high. The exploitability is told to be difficult. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The code maintainer explains: "I'm not going to commit some of the leak fixes I've been working on to the 2.44 branch due to concern that would destabilise ld. All of the reported leaks in this bugzilla have been fixed on binutils master."

A vulnerability was determined in GNU Binutils 2.45. The affected element is the function elf_x86_64_relocate_section of the file elf64-x86-64.c of the component Linker. This manipulation causes heap-based buffer overflow. The attack can only be executed locally. The exploit has been publicly disclosed and may be utilized. Patch name: 6b21c8b2ecfef5c95142cbc2c32f185cb1c26ab0. To fix this issue, it is recommended to deploy a patch.

An issue was discovered in Binutils before 2.46. The objdump contains a denial-of-service vulnerability when processing a crafted binary with malformed debug information. A logic flaw in the handling of DWARF location list headers can cause objdump to enter an unbounded loop and produce endless output until manually interrupted. This issue affects versions prior to the upstream fix and allows a local attacker to cause excessive resource consumption by supplying a malicious input file.

Binutils objdump contains a denial-of-service vulnerability when processing a crafted binary with malformed DWARF debug information. A logic error in the handling of DWARF compilation units can result in an invalid offset_size value being used inside byte_get_little_endian, leading to an abort (SIGABRT). The issue was observed in binutils 2.44. A local attacker can trigger the crash by supplying a malicious input file.

Binutils objdump contains a denial-of-service vulnerability when processing a crafted binary with malformed DWARF debug_rnglists data. A logic error in the handling of the debug_rnglists header can cause objdump to repeatedly print the same warning message and fail to terminate, resulting in an unbounded logging loop until the process is interrupted. The issue was observed in binutils 2.44. A local attacker can exploit this vulnerability by supplying a malicious input file, leading to excessive CPU and I/O usage and preventing completion of the objdump analysis.

GNU Binutils thru 2.45.1 readelf contains a denial-of-service vulnerability when processing a crafted binary with malformed DWARF loclists data. A logic flaw in the DWARF parsing code can cause readelf to repeatedly print the same table output without making forward progress, resulting in an unbounded output loop that never terminates unless externally interrupted. A local attacker can trigger this behavior by supplying a malicious input file, causing excessive CPU and I/O usage and preventing readelf from completing its analysis.

GNU Binutils thru 2.45.1 readelf contains a denial-of-service vulnerability when processing a crafted binary with malformed DWARF .debug_rnglists data. A logic flaw in the DWARF parsing path causes readelf to repeatedly print the same warning message without making forward progress, resulting in a non-terminating output loop that requires manual interruption. No evidence of memory corruption or code execution was observed.

GNU Binutils thru 2.46 readelf contains a vulnerability that leads to an invalid pointer free when processing a crafted ELF binary with malformed relocation or symbol data. If dump_relocations returns early due to parsing errors, the internal all_relocations array may remain partially uninitialized. Later, process_got_section_contents() may attempt to free an invalid r_symbol pointer, triggering memory corruption checks in glibc and causing the program to terminate with SIGABRT. No evidence of further memory corruption or code execution was observed; the impact is limited to denial of service. NOTE: this is disputed by third parties because the observed behavior occurred only in pre-release code and did not affect any tagged version.

GNU Binutils thru 2.46 readelf contains a vulnerability that leads to an abort (SIGABRT) when processing a crafted ELF binary with malformed DWARF abbrev or debug information. Due to incomplete state cleanup in process_debug_info(), an invalid debug_info_p state may propagate into DWARF attribute parsing routines. When certain malformed attributes result in an unexpected data length of zero, byte_get_little_endian() triggers a fatal abort. No evidence of memory corruption or code execution was observed; the impact is limited to denial of service.

A flaw was found in the GNU Binutils (Binary Utilities) linker. This vulnerability, a heap-buffer-overflow read (CWE-125), occurs when the linker processes a specially crafted 32-bit XCOFF (Extended Common Object File Format) object file. An attacker could exploit this by providing a malicious file, leading to an out-of-bounds read of memory. This can result in information disclosure, potentially revealing sensitive heap data, and a Denial of Service (DoS) due to the linker crashing.

Multiple Use-After-Free vulnerabilities were found in the add_archive_element function in ld/ldmain.c of the GNU linker (ld), a component of binutils. The root cause is that plugin_maybe_claim() in ld/plugin.c frees the original BFD object via bfd_close/_bfd_delete_bfd when entry->the_bfd->my_archive == NULL, but the caller retains both the original abfd parameter and a shallow copy (orig_input.the_bfd) as dangling pointers. These dangling pointers are subsequently dereferenced at three distinct locations in add_archive_element: 1. Line ~1442: accessing abfd->my_archive via bfd_usrdata(abfd->my_archive) 2. Line ~1493: multiple accesses to abfd and abfd->my_archive in a conditional check and bfd_get_filename call 3. Line ~1525: dereferencing the shallow copy orig_input.the_bfd->my_archive in trace/verbose logging The vulnerability is triggered when LTO plugins are active (link_info.lto_plugin_active is true) and the input object has abfd->my_archive == NULL, which is a valid state for standalone object files. Red Hat builds binutils with --enable-plugins and --enable-lto, confirming the vulnerable code path is compiled in and reachable. An attacker who can supply a crafted object or archive file to a build process using LTO-enabled linking could exploit this flaw to cause a denial of service (linker crash via segmentation fault). Arbitrary code execution is theoretically possible through heap manipulation but is substantially mitigated by hardening measures including stack protector, FORTIFY_SOURCE, ASLR, and PIE. The attack surface is limited to build-time environments — the linker is a development tool not exposed in production runtime. The most realistic exploitation scenario is a supply chain attack introducing a crafted object file as a build dependency in CI/CD pipelines or development environments.

A flaw was found in GNU Binutils. This heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability, specifically an out-of-bounds read in the bfd linker, allows an attacker to gain access to sensitive information. By convincing a user to process a specially crafted XCOFF object file, an attacker can trigger this flaw, potentially leading to information disclosure or an application level denial of service.

A flaw was found in GNU Binutils. This vulnerability, a heap-based buffer overflow, specifically an out-of-bounds read, exists in the bfd linker component. An attacker could exploit this by convincing a user to process a specially crafted malicious XCOFF object file. Successful exploitation may lead to the disclosure of sensitive information or cause the application to crash, resulting in an application level denial of service.

A flaw was found in the GNU Binutils BFD library, a widely used component for handling binary files such as object files and executables. The issue occurs when processing specially crafted XCOFF object files, where a relocation type value is not properly validated before being used. This can cause the program to read memory outside of intended bounds. As a result, affected tools may crash or expose unintended memory contents, leading to denial-of-service or limited information disclosure risks.

A flaw was found in the `readelf` utility of the binutils package. A local attacker could exploit two Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerabilities by providing a specially crafted Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) file. One vulnerability, a resource exhaustion (CWE-400), can lead to an out-of-memory condition. The other, a null pointer dereference (CWE-476), can cause a segmentation fault. Both issues can result in the `readelf` utility becoming unresponsive or crashing, leading to a denial of service.

A flaw was found in binutils, specifically within the `readelf` utility. This vulnerability allows a local attacker to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by tricking a user into processing a specially crafted Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) file. The exploitation of this flaw can lead to the system becoming unresponsive due to excessive resource consumption or a program crash.

A flaw was found in binutils. A heap-buffer-overflow vulnerability exists when processing a specially crafted XCOFF (Extended Common Object File Format) object file during linking. A local attacker could trick a user into processing this malicious file, which could lead to arbitrary code execution, allowing the attacker to run unauthorized commands, or cause a denial of service, making the system unavailable.

A path traversal vulnerability was identified in ReFirm Labs binwalk from version 2.1.2b through 2.3.3 inclusive. By crafting a malicious PFS filesystem file, an attacker can get binwalk's PFS extractor to extract files at arbitrary locations when binwalk is run in extraction mode (-e option). Remote code execution can be achieved by building a PFS filesystem that, upon extraction, would extract a malicious binwalk module into the folder .config/binwalk/plugins. This vulnerability is associated with program files src/binwalk/plugins/unpfs.py. This issue affects binwalk from 2.1.2b through and including 2.3.3.
vulnerabilities.summary: Path traversal in binwalk

vulnerabilities.details: A security vulnerability has been detected in OSPG binwalk up to 2.4.3. This vulnerability affects the function read_null_terminated_string of the file src/binwalk/plugins/winceextract.py of the component WinCE Extraction Plugin. Such manipulation of the argument self.file_name leads to path traversal. The attack can only be performed from a local environment. The exploit has been disclosed publicly and may be used. The project maintainer confirms this issue: "I accept the existence of the Path Traversal vulnerability. However, as stated in the Github link, it reached EOL and as a result no actions should be expected." The GitHub repository mentions, that "[u]sers and contributors should migrate to binwalk v3." This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

CVE-2026-111497 ("Node2Shell") is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) in Google's
Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c). DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns an ambiguous
value for an invalid block switch, and the fast decode path discards it
(CWE-252, unchecked return value), so a crafted Brotli stream makes the decoder
continue on corrupted state and write past the ring buffer. Upstream rates it
CVSS 4.0 9.2 and classifies the impact as potential remote code execution.

The vulnerability is in Google's C library, not in Node.js specifically. The
PyPI `Brotli` package is Google's CPython binding and compiles the same
c/dec/decode.c that has the actual vulnerability. All `Brotli` releases up to
and including 1.2.0 ship the vulnerable decoder; 1.2.1 contains the upstream
fix (commit 0ed4268a) and differs from 1.2.0 only in that fix plus a version
bump.

The decoder is reached whenever untrusted Brotli data is decompressed. With
`Brotli` installed, common HTTP clients decode Brotli responses automatically
(urllib3/requests, httpx with the brotli extra, aiohttp) and services that
accept `Content-Encoding: br` request bodies decode inbound data, so the flaw
is reachable from attacker-controlled input.
vulnerabilities.summary: Out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder ("Node2Shell") also affects the PyPI Brotli package

vulnerabilities.details:
A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.

Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.
vulnerabilities.summary: Brotli: Out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder ("Node2Shell") also affects the PyPI Brotli package

vulnerabilities.details:
This update removes the "emSign ECC Root CA - G3" CA certificate due to
intermediate CA certificates being compromised.

In addition, in Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, and Ubuntu 26.04 LTS,
the ca-certificates package contained outdated CA certificates. This update
refreshes the included certificates to those contained in the 2.90 version
of the Mozilla certificate authority bundle.
vulnerabilities.summary: ca-certificates update

vulnerabilities.details:
Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them. 

An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.

Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.
vulnerabilities.summary: certifi bundles emSign root CAs with compromised intermediate CA keys

authentication state when CURLOPT_AWS_SIGV4 was set to NULL. An attacker

sending credentials to the proxy itself by responding to a CONNECT
request with an unexpected authentication challenge. An attacker could

(CVE-2026-86414)

Stanislav Fort discovered that curl did not correctly handle HSTS
entries when an includeSubDomains parent entry was imported before a
longer-lived child entry. An attacker could possibly use this issue to
cause curl to use unencrypted HTTP connections. This issue only affected
Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-87862)

values that exceeded calendar time structure bounds. An attacker could
possibly use this issue to cause a denial of service or data loss. This
issue only affected Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-87863)

commands when CURLOPT_CRLF was enabled, allowing overflow bytes to be

possibly use this issue to inject arbitrary IMAP commands.
(CVE-2026-87864)

properly validate transfer directions, allowing a malicious server to

when processing deeply nested MIME structures. An attacker could
possibly use this issue to cause curl to crash, resulting in a denial of
service. This issue only affected Ubuntu 18.04 LTS, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS,
Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-92391)

vulnerabilities.details: diff3 tool from GNU diffutils is vulnerable to a heap‑based buffer overflow due to multiple signed integer overflows in line‑mapping calculations. Incorrect arithmetic in mapping line ranges can result in corrupted values being used for memory allocation and loop bounds. When processing crafted diff output, these overflows may cause the application to allocate insufficient memory and subsequently perform out‑of‑bounds writes during internal processing. An attacker who can control the output of the diff program used by diff3 (e.g. via --diff-program pointing to a malicious script) can trigger out-of-bounds writes, resulting in a crash and potentially remote code execution depending on the environment. This issue has been fixed in commit 9ff04d5b84743e331e80b589335a52c5480d1815 NOTE: The project maintainers claim that this is not a security issue. They state that the worst outcome this issue can cause is a crash of diff and that it cannot be used to escalate privileges.

On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.

Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 2.5 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.

Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on an unheld marker that another account can open.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, `AsyncSoftFileLock` and the other async soft locks, and `FileLock` after its `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `WindowsFileLock` opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover.
- Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with `os.open`, which on Windows applies no more of `mode` than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete.
- Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails.
- Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time.
- What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits.
- Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes.
- Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L84-L122) renames at L116 and unlinks at L118 and L122, by path. [`_poll_until_acquired`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1378-L1408) and [`_check_give_up`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1590-L1608) test the deadline, `blocking` and `cancel_check` only between attempts.

## Introduced

[e35c3af](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/e35c3af) "feat(soft): detect and break stale locks" ([#476](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/476), 2026-02-13), first tag 3.22.0 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.

## Mechanism

Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.

A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.

## Reproduction

The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. They ran on a Windows 11 VM (NTFS, CPython 3.14.8) against the head of PR #835 at `3e4c5ef`, where `_read_lock_file` and `break_lock_file` are the same code as at `b831496b0273` apart from import changes. The second account `fltester` is a member of `Users`; the directory grants it `(OI)(CI)(M)`.

**`oplock_vm.py`**

```python
"""
Windows oplock checks beyond the lock-file open PR #835 changes: release() and the soft locks' marker read.

Run on the VM (PowerShell, from the synced worktree, with the fltester account present):
  C:\\venvs\\rev4F\\Scripts\\python.exe oplock_vm.py fltester '<password>' C:\\tmp\\rev4F-oplock

[1] A second account keeps requesting a Level 1 oplock on the lock file through a read handle that shares delete.
    WindowsFileLock._release closes its handle and then unlinks by path; an oplock granted in between makes the
    DeleteFileW inside os.unlink wait for the holder's acknowledgement. [1a] races the close-to-unlink window as is;
    [1b] widens that window to 200 ms with a patched os.unlink so the grant lands inside it.
[2] A second account holds a Level 1 oplock on a soft-lock marker whose holder is alive. SoftFileLock.acquire reads the
    marker through os.open, which waits for the acknowledgement, past timeout=1.

A thread that exits has its pending oplock request cancelled, so every holder thread stays alive until the end.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import ctypes
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time
from ctypes import wintypes

from filelock import FileLock, SoftFileLock, Timeout

user, password, base = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
icacls = os.path.join(os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"], "System32", "icacls.exe")
os.makedirs(base, exist_ok=True)
subprocess.run([icacls, base, "/grant", f"{user}:(OI)(CI)(M)"], check=True, capture_output=True)

advapi32 = ctypes.WinDLL("advapi32", use_last_error=True)
kernel32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)
advapi32.LogonUserW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.HANDLE),
]
kernel32.CreateFileW.restype = kernel32.CreateEventW.restype = wintypes.HANDLE
kernel32.CreateFileW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.HANDLE,
]


class Overlapped(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = (
        ("Internal", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("InternalHigh", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("Offset", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("OffsetHigh", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("hEvent", wintypes.HANDLE),
    )


kernel32.DeviceIoControl.argtypes = [
    wintypes.HANDLE,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    ctypes.POINTER(Overlapped),
]
kernel32.CloseHandle.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE]
kernel32.WaitForSingleObject.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE, wintypes.DWORD]

GENERIC_READ = 0x80000000
SHARE_ALL = 0x7
OPEN_EXISTING = 3
FLAG_OVERLAPPED = 0x40000000
INVALID_HANDLE = wintypes.HANDLE(-1).value
FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1 = 0x00090000
ERROR_IO_PENDING = 997
hold = threading.Event()
real_unlink = os.unlink


def impersonate() -> None:
    token = wintypes.HANDLE()
    if not advapi32.LogonUserW(user, ".", password, 3, 0, ctypes.byref(token)):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())
    if not advapi32.ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(token):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())


def request_level1(path: str) -> tuple[int, Overlapped] | None:
    handle = kernel32.CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, SHARE_ALL, None, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED, None)
    if handle == INVALID_HANDLE:
        return None
    overlapped = Overlapped(hEvent=kernel32.CreateEventW(None, True, False, None))
    if (
        not kernel32.DeviceIoControl(handle, FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1, None, 0, None, 0, None, ctypes.byref(overlapped))
        and ctypes.get_last_error() == ERROR_IO_PENDING
    ):
        return handle, overlapped
    kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(overlapped.hEvent)
    return None


def drop(granted: tuple[int, Overlapped]) -> None:
    handle, overlapped = granted
    kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    kernel32.WaitForSingleObject(overlapped.hEvent, 5000)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(overlapped.hEvent)


def release_under_oplock_requests(label: str, lock_path: str, cycles: int) -> bool:
    stop = threading.Event()
    granted_box: list[tuple[int, Overlapped]] = []

    def spinner() -> None:
        impersonate()
        while not stop.is_set():
            if (granted := request_level1(lock_path)) is not None:
                granted_box.append(granted)
                hold.wait()
                return

    releasing = threading.Event()
    release_durations: list[float] = []

    def owner() -> None:
        # thread_local locks release only on the acquiring thread, so acquire and release stay on this one
        for _ in range(cycles):
            lock = FileLock(lock_path, is_singleton=False)
            lock.acquire(timeout=5)
            started = time.monotonic()
            releasing.set()
            lock.release()
            releasing.clear()
            release_durations.append(time.monotonic() - started)
            if granted_box:
                return
```

```python
        ("InternalHigh", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("Offset", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("OffsetHigh", wintypes.DWORD),

kernel32.WaitForSingleObject.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE, wintypes.DWORD]

SHARE_ALL, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED = 0x7, 3, 0x40000000

def take(path: str, level: str) -> tuple[int, Overlapped]:

    kernel32.CloseHandle(granted[0])
    kernel32.WaitForSingleObject(granted[1].hEvent, 5000)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(granted[1].hEvent)


def timed(label: str, operation) -> None:  # noqa: ANN001

    def run() -> None:

    threading.Thread(target=run, daemon=True).start()
    done.wait(15)
    print(f"  {label}: {result[0]}")
    return done

    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY | os.O_BINARY))


def open_write(path: str) -> None:

def create_new(path: str) -> None:
    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_BINARY))

        ("os.open O_RDWR", open_write, False),

        ("os.utime by path", lambda p: os.utime(p, None), False),
```

## Failure sequence


## Evidence

Section `[2]` of `oplock_vm.py` acquired `soft.lock` as the test account, closed the holder's descriptor so the marker stayed with a live process id and no open handle, took a Level 1 oplock through the second account's read handle (`oplock granted: True`), and ran `SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False).acquire(timeout=1)` on a thread. The call returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s, before the holder closed. The review did not establish what ends the wait at 10 s in the two-account runs; section `[1a]` of the same script, with the second account's handle, shows the same 10 s. In the same-account probe (`oplock_semantics_vm.py`) the open returned only when the holder closed, still running at 15 s. The probe also shows that the failed exclusive create and `os.utime` by path return at once, so the wait is in the read and the break, not in the create attempt.

## Impact

Each `acquire()` of a soft lock that finds a marker another account holds an oplock on runs past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` until the holder answers or closes, 10 s per attempt in the recorded two-account runs. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.

## Workarounds

- Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows.
- Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits.
- No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.

vulnerabilities.details:
`UnixFileLock`, the backend of `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix, empties whatever regular file it finds at the lock path once it holds the `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file). With an explicit `mode` it also chmods that file (sets its permission bits), whether or not this acquire created it. Another local user who can rename or hard-link one of the files of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the lock path gets that file truncated by the lock user's next `acquire()`. A hard link is a second name for the same file. With a mode such as `0o666` the file, still owned by the lock user, also becomes readable and writable by that other user. The other user can then read and alter everything the lock user writes to it afterwards.

`O_NOFOLLOW`, the defence added for the symlink variant (CVE-2025-68146), does not see a renamed file or a hard link. The rename route needs the file's directory to be writable without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The hard-link route into a sticky directory such as `/tmp` needs `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`, a Linux kernel setting. Affected versions are every filelock release up to and including 4.2.0 (the truncation is as old as the project; the chmod since 3.10.2).

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:

- `ANT-2026-KO573NWI` [high, CWE-706]: UnixFileLock truncates and chmods victim files renamed onto the lock path.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N` scores 6.1 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): one rename or link, then wait for the lock user's next acquire; no race. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the lock user's own process truncates a file it did not mean to touch, including content behind a second name the other user could neither modify nor delete. With a permissive explicit `mode` the other user can then write to it. If that file is one the lock user later executes or trusts, that is code execution as the lock user. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the old content is gone before the other user can read anything, but what the lock user writes afterwards through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file) it still holds is readable. `A:N` (no availability impact). `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on another user controlling names in a non-sticky directory on the lock's filesystem (or on `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`). The scanner rated this high. The maintainers score it medium because the reachable targets depend on the directory layout and kernel settings described below.

## Scope and preconditions

- Lock classes: `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix (`UnixFileLock`). `SoftFileLock` applies an explicit mode only to a file it created with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and does not truncate an existing file. `WindowsFileLock` has not truncated at any version.
- The other user must put a regular file of the lock user at the lock path before the lock user's next acquire, while the lock file does not exist yet. That is the case on first use, after a reboot, after a `/tmp` cleaner, or after a release with the default `preserve_lock_file=False`, which unlinks the file. The scanner checked three ways at the scanned commit, with default kernel settings unless stated:
  - rename inside a directory without the sticky bit (a group-writable project or cache directory, a root-created `0777` directory);
  - rename from such a directory into a sticky one (`1777`) on the same filesystem. The sticky bit only protects entries that already exist, so the move succeeds while the lock path is free. Once the lock user's lock file exists there, the same move fails with `EPERM`;
  - `link(2)` into a sticky directory. This needs a system that lets a user hard-link a file it cannot write, which on Linux means `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. Mainstream distributions set 1, which refuses the link. The scanner did not test macOS or the BSDs.
- What the lock user loses: with the default `FileLock(path)` the lock truncates the file, which keeps its mode. With an explicit `mode` (a lock shared between users needs `0o666` or `0o660`, because `UnixFileLock` opens the file read-write), the lock also chmods the file to that mode. `_apply_explicit_mode` suppresses `PermissionError` only for files the lock user does not own. The lock user owns its own files, so the `fchmod` succeeds.
- Trust boundary: the protection against another local user holds only when no other user can rename entries in the lock's directory or, for the rename-into-sticky route, in any directory on the same filesystem that holds a file of the lock user. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against.
- Not affected: a symlink (a file that points at another path) at the lock path, because `O_NOFOLLOW` makes the open fail with `ELOOP`; mutual exclusion between cooperating processes.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L144-L163), whose [`os.ftruncate` and `_apply_explicit_mode` calls](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L150-L154) have only the `st_nlink != 0` guard (the file still has at least one name); [`_apply_explicit_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L165-L168); [`_open_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L95-L121), which learns from its `O_EXCL` create whether this attempt made the file but hands that flag only to the `ENOSYS` fallback.

## Introduced

The truncation of whatever is at the lock path dates from the initial commit ([2157efb](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/2157efb8b57666699fcf15bf03c3771c1571279c), which opened with `O_TRUNC`). The chmod of a pre-existing inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) came with [d7e1e84](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d7e1e84e71ad) "changed from os.umask to os.chmod" ([#206](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/206), 2023-03-22), first tag 3.10.2 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it the code passed the mode only to `open()`, which applies it to a file this call creates. The advisory range is therefore every release up to 4.2.0. The earlier group range `>= 3.10.0` understated it, as the review noted.

## Mechanism

`_open_lock_file` first tries `os.open(path, O_RDWR | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CREAT | O_EXCL, mode)`. With the lock user's file renamed to the lock path that fails with `FileExistsError`. The second `os.open(path, O_RDWR | O_NOFOLLOW)` succeeds, because the entry is a regular file the lock user owns, and returns `created = False`. `_acquire_native` passes `created` only to the `ENOSYS` branch. No process holds a `flock` on the renamed file, so `_lock_fd_nonblocking(fd)` succeeds at once and `_finalize_locked_fd(fd)` runs: `os.fstat`, `st_nlink != 0`, `os.ftruncate(fd, 0)`, then `os.fchmod(fd, mode)` when the lock has an explicit mode. Nothing in that path tells a lock file from any other regular file; a link count of 2 and a non-empty file both pass. `O_NOFOLLOW` does not help because the entry is the file itself (or a hard link, an ordinary directory entry for the same inode), not a symlink to it. There is no race: the other user renames or links once and waits for the next acquire. `AsyncUnixFileLock` inherits `_finalize_locked_fd` unchanged.

The scanner measured three variants at the same commit, same accounts (`victim` uid 1000, `attacker` uid 1001). First, a rename within a `0777` directory: the next `FileLock("jobs.lock", mode=0o666)` of `victim` empties the `0600` journal of `victim` renamed to `jobs.lock` and sets it to `0666`; `attacker` then reads what `victim` keeps writing through its open descriptor. Second, a rename of a two-name file (`ln /tmp/cache/blob ~/env/blob`, `0644`) from a `0777` directory, `fs.protected_hardlinks=1`: after `mv /tmp/cache/blob /tmp/cache/app.lock` and `FileLock("/tmp/cache/app.lock", mode=0o666)` as `victim`, `~/env/blob` has `2 links, mode 666, 0 bytes` and `echo pwned >> /home/victim/env/blob` as `attacker` succeeds, in a directory `attacker` cannot write. Third, `os.link(notes, lock_path)` in a `1777` directory with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`: `notes.txt` (`0644`, in the home of `victim`) ends up 0 bytes with mode `0666`, and `open(notes, "w")` as `attacker` then succeeds. With plain `FileLock(lock_path)` a `0600` file ends up empty with its mode unchanged. The planted name stays after release, so every later acquire truncates the file again.

```python
    print("done", flush=True)
```

## Evidence

The scanner reproducer (`victim` and `attacker` accounts, root-created `0777` directory without the sticky bit under `/tmp`, default sysctls, Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14.8, overlayfs; lock `FileLock(path, mode=0o666, timeout=5)`). It printed `CONTROL journal: inode 296383, uid 1000, mode 600, content 'ran job 1\n'` and `CONTROL attacker reads the journal: 'permission denied\n'`. After the rename and the second job of `victim` it printed `OBSERVED lock path: inode 296383, uid 1000, mode 666, content 'ran job 2 f4bc9a4e04c3f556\n'` and `OBSERVED attacker reads the lock path: 'ran job 2 f4bc9a4e04c3f556\n'`, last line `BUG`. The verdict requires that the earlier read by `attacker` failed, that the lock path is the journal's inode, that the old line is gone, that the mode went from `0600` to `0666`, and that the later read by `attacker` contains the secret. It runs in under a second with no race. The scanner ran the two-name and `link(2)` variants above by hand at the same commit (commands and results in its report), not through the script.

Maintainer triage: the reproducer prints `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 release image. The independent review (`soft-open`) confirmed the mechanism and that the hard-link and two-name variants go through the same two calls.

## Impact

The file's content is lost in every configuration, including for processes that hold the file open and under every other name the file has. With an explicit permissive `mode`, the other user can read and modify everything the lock user writes afterwards, while the file still belongs to the lock user. The other user can rename the file back to its old name after the acquire. It stays there with the lock's mode, and the lock user's next acquire creates a fresh lock file.

Somebody who may rename a single-name file may also unlink it, so losing such a file under its name is not new. What the lock adds are two operations on the inode that the other user cannot perform, `ftruncate` and `fchmod`, run with the lock user's privileges. Those matter for a descriptor the lock user still holds, for a second name of the file, and for programs that trust the file's ownership. The other user does not choose the mode, and the lock user writes no bytes the other user chose. Mutual exclusion is not affected.

## Workarounds

- Keep the lock file in a directory no other account can write, or in a sticky directory on a filesystem where no directory holding the lock user's files is writable by others. On Linux keep `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (the default on mainstream distributions), which closes the hard-link route.
- Do not pass a permissive explicit `mode` (`0o666`, `0o660`, `0o644`) unless accounts share the lock; without a mode the exposure is the truncation only.
- Keep the lock file in place (`preserve_lock_file=True`). Once a lock file owned by the lock user exists in a sticky directory, another user cannot rename or link over it.
- Where the lock does not need `flock` semantics, `SoftFileLock` applies its mode only to the marker it created with `O_EXCL` and does not truncate an existing file.

vulnerabilities.details:
filelock on Windows ignores the `mode` argument. `FileLock(path, mode=0o600)` creates the same file as `FileLock(path)`: one with no security descriptor of its own (the Windows record that says who may access a file). Its access list, or ACL, is whatever the lock directory hands down to new files. filelock creates the `ReadWriteLock` database, which it asks to be `0o600`, the same way. In a directory whose inheritable ACL grants other local accounts access to new files, those accounts can open the lock file or database. They can take the byte-range lock (a lock on a span of bytes in a file) once the owner releases it and keep the owner's later `acquire()` calls waiting or timing out. They can read holder metadata an `on_acquired` hook left in a `preserve_lock_file=True` file. Where the directory hands down modify access, they can write to both files.

`lock.mode` still reports `0o600`. The documentation neither promises an ACL on Windows nor says that Windows drops the mode. On Unix the same mode keeps other accounts out. Mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol holds on either platform. Affected versions are filelock 3.10.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:

- `ANT-2026-0KEO0DDO` [medium, CWE-732]: WindowsFileLock ignores mode; 0o600 lock files inherit the directory ACL.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L` scores 5.3 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): no race. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the lock file (holder metadata) and the lock database are readable where `0o600` was meant to keep them private. `I:L` (partial integrity impact): in the directory layout the maintainers tested, the other account can also write both files, which lets it corrupt the lock's own state but nothing the lock protects. `A:L` (partial availability impact): the other account can hold the byte-range lock and make the owner wait or time out. `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the review: **Windows permission failure with security impact only where callers rely on `mode=0o600` across accounts**. The review had marked it an unconfirmed Windows claim, since the scanner traced stand-in Win32 calls on Linux. The maintainers have since confirmed it on Windows with two local accounts (see Evidence). The scanner rated this medium; the maintainers keep medium.

## Scope and preconditions

- The affected classes are `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Windows (`WindowsFileLock`), and the SQLite database of `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`. Both go through `_open_non_reparse_fd`. The soft locks create their markers with `os.open`, which also keeps only a read-only bit of the mode on Windows; the scanner did not examine them further.
- The directory is one that other local accounts cannot write, which the documentation already requires on Windows, but whose inheritable entries grant them read (or modify) access to new files. Examples are a service's data directory readable by `Users`, or any directory with `(OI)(CI)` entries (entries that new files and sub-directories inherit) for another account. A directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts, such as one inside a user profile, hides the problem.
- The other account must open the file. According to the `LockFileEx` documentation, read access is enough to take the byte-range lock, so it can hold the lock whenever the owner does not. The lock file exists while the owner holds the lock, and stays after release with `preserve_lock_file=True`. The `ReadWriteLock` database is not unlinked at any point.
- Unix is not affected, because `UnixFileLock` creates the file with the mode and repeats it with `fchmod`. Mutual exclusion between cooperating processes is not affected.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_open_non_reparse_fd` reduces the mode to one `read_only` bit](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L252-L253). That bit is false for every accepted mode, because [`_check_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L526) rejects any mode without owner read and write, and an unset mode becomes `0o666`. In [`_nt_open`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L283-L310) the `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES.SecurityDescriptor` field stays unassigned, and `read_only` only chooses `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY`. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1086) passes `0o600` through the same function on Windows.

## Introduced

[d0061e4](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d0061e4643df) "added multiuser support and associated tests" ([#192](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/192), 2023-03-15), first tag 3.10.0 (verified), added the `mode` parameter and on Windows handed it to `os.open`, which applies only the read-only attribute. The Windows backend has applied no more of the mode than that at any version, so this is a long-standing gap rather than a regression.

## Mechanism

`_open_non_reparse_fd(path, mode)` computes `read_only = not mode & _OWNER_WRITE` and calls `_nt_open(path, read_only=read_only)`. `_nt_open` fills an `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` with the NT path and `OBJ_CASE_INSENSITIVE` and leaves `SecurityDescriptor` NULL. It then calls `NtCreateFile` with `FILE_OPEN_IF` and `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL` (or `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY` when `read_only`, which no accepted mode produces). Nothing consults the group and other bits. Per the `NtCreateFile` and `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` documentation, a NULL descriptor gives the new file default security, which on NTFS is the set of inheritable entries of the parent directory. A lock file created with `mode=0o600` in a directory that hands down read access to `Users` is therefore readable by `Users`.

Nothing tells the caller. The constructor validates the mode, `lock.mode` returns `0o600`, and `has_explicit_mode` is `True`. `docs/concepts.rst` says "filelock creates the file with it" and that "`0o600` and `0o700` keep other UIDs out", with no Windows caveat. Only the `_open_non_reparse_fd` docstring and a comment in `_soft.py` record the limitation.

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs on a Linux image. It imports filelock's unmodified Windows backend with `sys.platform == "win32"` over stand-ins that print every Win32 call. The program with `mode=0o600` and the one without produce identical call lists (`RtlDosPathNameToNtPathName_U_WithStatus`, `NtCreateFile` with `FileAttributes=0x80` and `ObjectAttributes.SecurityDescriptor=None`, `RtlFreeUnicodeString`, `GetFileInformationByHandle`, `LockFileEx`, `UnlockFileEx`), while the Unix control produced `0o600` and `0o644` files. It prints `OBSERVED the two Win32 call lists are identical: True` and `BUG`. The scanner stated that it inferred the resulting ACL, and what another user can then do, from the documentation and did not run on Windows.

Maintainer triage: the stand-in reproducer prints `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 release image.

Maintainer verification on Windows 11 with two local accounts: a script creates `private.lock` with `FileLock(mode=0o600, preserve_lock_file=True)`, `default.lock` without a mode, and a `ReadWriteLock` database `lock.db` as the first account, in a directory granted `(OI)(CI)(M)` to a second account that is a member of `Users`. It then opens each file under the second account's logon token with `LogonUserW` and `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser`. On 4.2.0 the second account could open `private.lock` and `lock.db` for both read and write, the same as `default.lock`, and `icacls` listed only inherited `(I)` entries on all three. This confirms the claim the review had marked unconfirmed.

## Impact

A program that passes `mode=0o600` so that other accounts cannot open its lock file gets no such restriction on Windows. In a directory that hands down read access, another account can hold the lock and make the owner wait or time out, and read holder metadata in a preserved lock file. Where the directory hands down modify access, as in the maintainers' test, it can also write the lock file and the `ReadWriteLock` database. With the mode honoured, as on Unix, a user without write access to the directory can do none of this. The exposure ends there: the effect reaches only the lock file or lock database, and mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol still holds.

## Workarounds

- On Windows, keep lock files and `ReadWriteLock` databases in a directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts (inside the user profile, or a directory with inheritance disabled and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted), rather than relying on `mode`.
- After creating a lock file with `preserve_lock_file=True` or a `ReadWriteLock` database, set its ACL yourself, for example `icacls <file> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:F" "SYSTEM:F" "Administrators:F"`; a file that exists keeps its ACL on later opens.
- Do not store anything confidential in the lock file through `on_acquired` on Windows.

vulnerabilities.summary: filelock: WindowsFileLock ignores mode: a 0o600 lock file and the ReadWriteLock database inherit the directory ACL

vulnerabilities.details:
On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: `<database>-journal`, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); `<database>-wal`, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and `<database>-shm`, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone `DELETE` on it, which a file's creator may do. `C:\Windows\Temp` (the temporary directory of services, granting `BUILTIN\Users` create but not delete) and `C:\Users\Public` are such directories.

With a `-wal` in place, every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at once, whatever `timeout` says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a `-journal` beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). It is not among the findings of the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 3.3 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): create one file beside the database and set its ACL (access control list); no race, and the other account can place the file days earlier. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account that can create files in the directory is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other account learns nothing. `I:N` (no integrity impact in the scored variant): see the scoring note. `A:L` (partial availability impact): every acquire fails with an exception that `Timeout` handlers do not catch, until the other account removes its file; no crash, and the lock's own data is not changed.

Scoring note. The deletion variant reads `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L` (3.6): `I:L` because the lock user's process deletes one file the journal names, `AC:H` because it needs a lock database that holds a table, which filelock does not create, and a journal the lock user can open for writing. The lower-reading rule of this advisory set scores the variant that reaches every `ReadWriteLock` on Windows in such a directory, 3.3, and describes the deletion variant under Mechanism. Classification from the review: **security** (another account), availability for the scored variant.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`, both of which connect through `_connect`. On Linux and macOS the lock takes other routes, covered by GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.
- Directory: one where another account can create files but cannot delete the lock user's. `C:\Windows\Temp` carries `BUILTIN\Users:(CI)(S,WD,AD,X)` (create file and create subdirectory, no delete child); `C:\Users\Public` and any directory with such an entry qualify. A directory only the lock user can write, such as `%LOCALAPPDATA%` or the per-user temporary directory, is not affected.
- The other account creates `<database>-wal`, grants everyone modify and denies everyone `DELETE` on it. A file's creator may set both. The lock user can open and read the file but not delete it.
- Deletion variant: the lock database holds at least one table (filelock creates an empty database, and the review's reproducer has the lock account create the table), and the other account's `<database>-journal` grants the lock account modify rights. The journal's tail names a file the lock user can delete.
- What the lock user sees: `write_lock(timeout=1)` raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` with the undeletable `-wal` in place; with the writable journal the acquire succeeded and the named file was gone; with an undeletable journal every acquire raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file`.
- The documentation at the scanned commit states "the lock directory must not be writable by untrusted users" for `WindowsFileLock`, in its symlink paragraph; the `ReadWriteLock` documentation names no directory requirement on Windows.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [Windows branch of `_connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L951-L965) checks the database through a handle and then calls `sqlite3.connect(database, ...)` with the path. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect that handle, not the side files. The first statement is [`PRAGMA busy_timeout=...; PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY;` at L816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). [`_do_acquire_inner` at L763](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) turns only `"database is locked"` into `Timeout`; any other `sqlite3.OperationalError` leaves the acquire.

## Introduced

[cfd4446](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/cfd4446) "feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock" ([#399](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/399), 2026-02-12), first tag 3.20.4 (verified with `git tag --contains`), passed the lock path to `sqlite3.connect` on every platform. The Linux descriptor route (4.0.9) and the macOS hard-link route (4.1.1) did not change Windows, where the connect has been by name in every release since. The reproducer ran against the head of PR #834 at `1f9e415`, whose Windows branch of `_connect` is the same code as at `b831496b0273`.

## Mechanism

`_connect` on Windows opens the database with `_open_non_reparse_fd`, checks through that handle that the file is a regular file, not a reparse point, and that its header does not declare WAL mode, and keeps the handle open while `sqlite3.connect(database)` opens the same name. The check covers the database, not the names beside it. On the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, SQLite takes its first lock on the database and looks for `<database>-wal`. A non-empty `-wal` beside a database that is not in WAL mode is a leftover SQLite deletes. The other account's file denies `DELETE`, so the pragma raises `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`, which reaches the caller as `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. `_do_acquire_inner` converts only "database is locked" into `Timeout`, so `acquire_read()`, `acquire_write()` and the async forms raise at once, on every call, until the file is gone. The lock user has no right to delete it.

The journal variant needs a database with content. Beside a non-empty database SQLite treats a `<database>-journal` with a valid header as hot (left by an interrupted write) and replays it before the first statement runs. The review's journal is 46 bytes: a file path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. That tail names a super-journal, and recovery ends by deleting the file it names. The lock user's `write_lock()` therefore deletes one file the other account chose, provided the lock user can delete it, and returns without error. SQLite opens a hot journal for writing, so the other account's journal must grant the lock account modify rights; a read-only journal makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` instead. GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8 describes the same side-file behavior on POSIX, where the sticky bit plays the part the directory ACL plays here.

## Evidence

The reproducer printed the three lines above on the VM: the undeletable `-wal` beside an empty database made `write_lock(timeout=1)` fail with `OperationalError: disk I/O error` and left the file in place; the writable journal beside a database with one table let the acquire succeed while the file the journal named, created by the lock account with the content `keep`, was gone along with the journal; the read-only journal made the acquire fail with `OperationalError: unable to open database file` and left both files. The review notes that the Windows branch of `_connect` is unchanged since #399, so the behavior is the same at `b831496b0273` and in 4.2.0. The scanner and the maintainers measured the same side-file effects on Linux for GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.

## Impact

In a directory such as `C:\Windows\Temp`, another local account turns every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` on a `ReadWriteLock` database into an immediate `sqlite3.OperationalError`, for as long as its file stays. Callers that handle `Timeout` or `OSError` do not catch it, and the lock user cannot remove the file. With a lock database that holds a table and a journal the lock user can write, the lock user's process deletes one file of the other account's choosing, among the files the lock user may delete, and the acquire reports success. The lock's own database is not changed, nothing is read, and mutual exclusion between processes that acquire the lock holds.

## Workarounds

- Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory other accounts cannot create files in: `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, the per-user temporary directory (`%TEMP%` of a user session), or a directory with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted. `C:\Windows\Temp` and `C:\Users\Public` do not qualify.
- Treat `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` on every acquire as a foreign `<database>-wal` beside the database, which only its creator or an administrator can remove.

vulnerabilities.summary: filelock: ReadWriteLock on Windows acts on SQLite side files another local user places beside its database

vulnerabilities.details:
`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) run `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` on a fresh connection for every acquire. That statement makes SQLite load the whole schema (the `sqlite_master` table, which lists every table and index with its `CREATE` text) of whatever file sits at the lock path. The caller's `timeout` reaches SQLite only as `busy_timeout`, which bounds waits for another connection's lock, not schema loading. The only content checks reject non-regular files and WAL mode (write-ahead log, an SQLite mode that keeps changes in a side file). A local user who can place or overwrite the file at a `ReadWriteLock`'s database path can therefore make every `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` of every process using that lock ignore its `timeout` and `blocking=False`. That position needs a non-sticky shared directory, or a database owned by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) that other users may write.

One 37 KB crafted file stalls each acquire for as long as its author chooses while the process allocates about 1 GB. A second 28 KB layout makes the acquire of a free lock run without end, spinning at 100% CPU and ignoring Ctrl-C. The effect is availability only: the other user reads nothing and corrupts nothing. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-NFPRHMYJ` [medium, CWE-400]: ReadWriteLock: crafted lock database hangs acquire regardless of timeout.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` scores 5.5 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the other user plants one file; no race. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `A:H` (high availability impact): every acquire of every process using the lock runs for as long as that user chose, or does not return, with `timeout` and `blocking=False` ignored and `SIGINT` not delivered, so only killing the process ends it. `C:N` and `I:N` (no confidentiality or integrity impact): the other user reads nothing and corrupts nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, an availability concern only when an untrusted actor can supply the database file (it needs a writable or replaceable database path). The scanner rated it medium. The review agrees with the mechanism and the precondition.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other party is a different local account that can create or replace the file at the lock path. One way: the lock directory is writable by that account and not sticky (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it), for example a group-writable project or cache directory. There the account can be the first to create the database, or rename the lock user's database aside and put the crafted one in its place. The other way: the lock user's own database is writable by that account (`0666`), which is the setup a lock shared between accounts needs. In a `1777` directory the scanner wrote the crafted file over such a database in place, and the lock user's next acquire hung. The lock user must be able to open the file read-write, so a file the other user creates is `0666`.
- Sticky directories and kernel settings. In a sticky world-writable directory such as `/tmp`, Linux with `fs.protected_regular=2` (a kernel setting) refuses the lock user's `O_CREAT` open of a file owned by the other account with `EACCES`. A database owned by the other user does not work there. That does not cover a `0666` database owned by the lock user. The scanner did not test systems with `fs.protected_regular=0` (the kernel's own default).
- Platform. Every platform runs the same statements. On Windows the documentation already requires a lock directory that untrusted users cannot write, so the shared-directory setup is outside what the project supports there.
- Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_configure_and_begin` runs `PRAGMA busy_timeout=...; PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY;` on a fresh connection](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L814-L816), and for a read lock [`SELECT name FROM sqlite_master LIMIT 1` at line 832](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L832). The code in [`_do_acquire_inner` closes the previous connection and opens a new one on every acquire](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L745-L754). The only content checks are [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) (regular file) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) (20 header bytes).

## Introduced

The acquire path dates from `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)", 2026-02-12), first released in **3.20.4** (verified: `git tag --contains cfd4446` gives 3.20.4). Since #657 (3.30.0) the lock reopens the connection on every acquire, so the stall repeats on every acquire rather than once per instance.

## Mechanism

`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` is the first statement that needs the schema. SQLite reads every row of `sqlite_master` and parses each row's `sql` text there. Run one at a time on the crafted file, `PRAGMA busy_timeout` returns at once and `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` takes the whole time. The read-mode `SELECT` needs the schema too. The caller's `timeout` reaches SQLite only as `busy_timeout` (lines 814 to 816 and 823 to 826), which limits how long SQLite waits for another connection's file lock. Loading the schema is not a wait, so nothing limits it. `blocking=False` and `timeout=0` reach SQLite as `busy_timeout=0` and stall the same way (2.4 s each with a 5-row file). `acquire_write` runs the same pragma. `AsyncReadWriteLock.read_lock(timeout=1)` stalls the same way (4.7 s with 10 rows; wrapping the acquire in `asyncio.wait_for(..., 2)` does not return earlier). A second `acquire_read` on the same instance stalls for as long as the first.

The constructor is not affected. Its validation connection (lines 484 and 485) runs no statement, so the lock user sees nothing until the first acquire. A stack dump taken 2 s into the stall shows the thread in `_configure_and_begin` at the `executescript` call. The lock accepts any SQLite file that is a regular file and not in WAL mode, whoever created it. Two layouts reach the load, at the same statement and with the same preconditions.

**Long schema rows.** Each `sqlite_master` row is `('table', 't0001', 't0001', 2, 'CREATE TABLE t0001(x) --AAAA…')` with an `sql` text of 999,999,024 bytes, under SQLite's 1,000,000,000-byte limit. The file does not store the text. Each row's cell names page 2 as its first overflow page (a page that holds the part of a row too large for its own page), and the "next overflow page" field of page 2 names page 2 again. SQLite builds each row from the same 4 KB page, read about 244,000 times over. The header claims 244,142 pages, because SQLite rejects a record larger than page size times page count. The script extends the file to that length as a hole (unallocated space that reads as zeros), because SQLite also rejects a file shorter than its header claims. Eight rows fit in one 4 KB leaf page. The statements are valid `CREATE TABLE`s, so SQLite reports no error, and after the stall the acquire succeeds; it does not raise `Timeout`.

Measured with `read_lock(timeout=1)`: 1 row, 12,288 bytes on disk, returns after 0.6 s; 10 rows, 16,384 bytes, 4.8 s; 50 rows, 36,864 bytes, 23 s. Peak RSS (resident set size, the memory the process holds) is 981 MB in every case, because memory stays at one row's worth; the cost is about 0.47 s per row. Under a 512 MiB address-space limit the same acquire raises `MemoryError` from line 816.

**Looping interior pages.** The long rows are one way in, not the cause: SQLite loads whatever schema the file holds, with no bound. A 20 KB file with no long rows, whose three index pages each point 200 times at the same child page (8,000,000 leaves), stalls `read_lock(timeout=1)` for 8 s with 10 MB of memory. Each extra level multiplies the time by the fan-out (the number of children per page).

At the largest fan-out SQLite accepts, the stall becomes a hang. In a 28,672-byte file of seven 4 KB pages, pages 1 to 6 are `sqlite_master` interior pages whose 660 cell pointers all name one 5-byte cell. That cell's child and the page's right-most child are both the next page, and page 7 is a leaf with one row of five NULLs. SQLite 3.40.1 refuses a page with more than 681 cells and a tree deeper than 20 pages, but does not notice that it reaches a page more than once. Each level therefore multiplies the rows of `sqlite_master` by 661.

The row is not a valid schema entry, and that does not stop the scan: SQLite raises `sqlite3.DatabaseError: malformed database schema (?)` only after the last row. One level raises `DatabaseError` at once. Two levels (12 KiB) give 436,921 rows after 0.16 s. Six levels (28 KiB) give 661⁶, about 8 × 10¹⁶ rows, still at line 816 with 30 s of CPU time used when killed after 30 s. On that file `acquire_write(timeout=1)`, `acquire_read(blocking=False)` and `acquire_read(timeout=0)` spin on the same line. `SIGINT` does not raise `KeyboardInterrupt` (the process was still running at 100% CPU 4 s after `kill -INT`), because the thread does not leave the one SQLite call.
